mitigation_mechanism: Trees and live fences carry livestock through drought as a fodder reserve: trees were the main source of animal feed and milk production for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought, and live fences of Gliricidia sepium, Leucaena leucocephala and similar species supply high-quality fodder when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. During drought, understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system even under intense shade, silvopastures are credited with better water infiltration rates, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].
caveats: The Zambian, US and Sahelian parkland units come from agro-pastoral systems, and the US silvopasture unit is high-income evidence that names infiltration rather than a drought outcome [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]; the understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, as tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. mitigation_mechanism: In two Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought, citing deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Trees also share deep water and act as a fodder reserve: hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots, millet with the shrub Guiera senegalensis in the Sahel produced over 900% more biomass under water stress, trees were the main source of feed and milk for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought, and in Senegal's sylvopastoral zone tree leaves, fruits and pods make up about 40 per cent of cattle diet before the rains [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. In an induced drought in eastern Canada only the monocrop lost yield, agroforestry biomass in the Brazilian semi-arid varied far less over 4 years than conventional systems, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. In Cañas, Costa Rica, cattle on pasture with high tree density gained 2 to 5% more weight in the dry season than those on low-cover pasture, attributed partly to longer grazing and rumination under reduced heat stress [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].

mitigation_mechanism: Under drought, shade over cocoa and coffee has been found to protect the crop, to compete with it for water, and to make no difference. On the protective side, in a throughfall-exclusion experiment in Ghana, cocoa dry bean yield was 12 to 45% higher under shade than in full sun at every level of rainwater suppression [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1]; in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly positive for coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; and reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]. On the competing side, reviews cite that under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms, that drought caused greater water loss in cacao agroforests than in open-sun cacao because trees and cacao both transpire, and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_9, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]. Between them sit three no-effect findings: in the Ghana experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline and only partly compensated for it [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and across cabruca cocoa farms in southern Bahia, Brazil, drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2].
caveats: What separates the sides, as far as the evidence says, is twofold. First, a higher yield under shade is not the same as protection from drought: the Ghana experiment shows both at once, with yield higher under shade at every drought level but the drought loss itself not buffered [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. mitigation_mechanism: Trees were the most important source of animal feed and milk for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought, and agroforestry in Brazil's semi-arid region had much less year-to-year variation in biomass productivity than conventional systems, attributed mainly to water availability [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6]. A US silvopasture study lists better water infiltration among silvopasture's services [ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. In Cañas, Costa Rica, cattle on pasture with high tree density gained 2 to 5% more weight in the dry season than those on low-cover pasture, attributed partly to longer grazing and rumination under reduced heat stress [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3].
caveats: The evidence is adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target: the Zambian unit is low income, the Brazilian and Colombian units are upper-middle income, and the US and Costa Rican units are high income [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Every unit is reported second-hand or as a background statement, and the US unit is a soil-water component proxy that does not mention drought [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9]. The Latin American silvopastoral units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The deep-root forage and dry-season liveweight units describe the dry season and give no drought-loss measure [ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3].

mitigation_mechanism: On rainfed cropland the evidence divides on whether trees add water the crop can use or compete with the crop for it. Hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots, and in the Sahel millet intercropped with the shrub Guiera senegalensis produced over 900% more biomass under water stress [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1]. In an experimentally induced drought in eastern Canada, crop losses occurred in the monocrop only, not in the soybean intercropping agroforestry system, and during drought understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system even under intense shade [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]; the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the El Niño-associated drought of 1997, while farmers who had not adopted it suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2].
caveats: The sub-practices disagree, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence. On the gain side, regeneration-based farmland holds the stronger result and reads as a benefit throughout: Sahelian parkland trees make deep soil moisture available to crop roots, the FMNR compiler rates drought impacts as mitigated, Quesungual crops withstood the 1997 drought, and Ethiopian wheat under Faidherbia albida out-yielded open-field wheat in the El Niño year, a hazard-year result kept apart from the study's normal-season gain [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. On the conflicting side, planted silvoarable systems pair gains (the Canadian induced drought, the Sahelian millet–Guiera result, the Ethiopian programme rating, German alley-cropping soil water) with a reversal, Kenyan maize under Grevillea robusta, where competition for limited soil water delayed flowering and can lead to crop failure [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]; and boundary plantings pair a live-fence fodder role in drought with greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years and a Senegal review that finds no consensus on windbreak hedges in drought [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. What separates the sides in the units' own words is whether tree roots reach moisture the crop cannot, or compete with the crop for limited soil water close to the trees. The understorey drought-year result and the Nigerian income model sit outside the voting sub-practices: the understorey benefit reverses under normal rainfall, and the income model found no significant drought effect [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The Canadian result is high-income temperate evidence, the Ethiopian unit rates a bundled sustainable land management programme, the live-fence fodder unit is a pantropical review, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating rather than a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The German soil-water difference was not significant at all positions and is high-income evidence, and the Honduran point is an earlier finding cited in an ICRAF working paper [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3].

mitigation_mechanism: Woody plants in a crop field under drought have been found both to protect the crop and to compete with it for water. On the protective side, in the Sahel millet intercropped with the shrub Guiera senegalensis produced over 900% more biomass under water stress, in a study set up to test whether hydraulic redistribution by the shrub benefits the crop [ev_crop_yield_santos25_1]; in an experimentally induced drought in eastern Canada, crop losses occurred in the monocrop only, not in the soybean intercropping agroforestry system [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]; and in a German alley-cropping system in a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though not significantly at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. On the competing side, in Kenyan maize with Grevillea robusta, competition for limited soil water delayed maize flowering and development and can lead to crop failure [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]. In the Ethiopian Highlands, income growth through commercial agroforestry was also named as an option that reduced drought vulnerability in some communities [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4].
caveats: What separates the two sides, as far as the evidence says, is whether the woody species and the crop draw on the same limited soil water: the loss is attributed to that competition in a maize and Grevillea system [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10], whereas the largest gain is with a shrub studied for its redistribution of water to the crop [ev_crop_yield_santos25_1]. The choice of tree and crop combination is therefore the design question for drought-exposed rainfed cropping. Both sides carry weaknesses. The 900% figure is a single study cited in a review; the Canadian and German results are high-income temperate evidence, and the German one was not significant at all positions [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]; the Ethiopian unit is a stakeholder rating of a bundled sustainable land management programme (terracing, bunds, area closure, small-scale irrigation, agroforestry), not attributable to agroforestry alone [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4]. mitigation_mechanism: Evidence that trees lessen drought impacts in tree-crop systems comes from shaded cocoa and coffee and from general agroforestry reports. For shaded cocoa and coffee: in a throughfall-exclusion experiment in Ghana, cocoa dry bean yield was 12 to 45% higher under shade than in full sun at every level of rainwater suppression [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1]; in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly positive for coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; and reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]. A review adds that under normal rainfall tree shade can lower understorey crop yields, while during drought those yields can be higher than in an open system, even in intense shade [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. In Lempira, Honduras, crops on farms using the Quesungual agroforestry system withstood the particularly severe 1997 drought while non-adopters suffered crop losses [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3]; live fences supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]; the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]; and in Ethiopia's sustainable land management programme, income from commercial agroforestry was named as one option that reduced drought vulnerability in some communities [ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4].
caveats: No-benefit and harm findings discount the class. In the Ghana experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on cocoa yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced decline; the Ethiopian coffee study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in extreme climate shocks; on Bahia cocoa farms drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover; and a model cited in a review found no significant impact on Nigerian agroforestry household net revenues under a simulated warmer, drier climate [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_household_income_watts22_14]. The harm findings are all second-hand readings in reviews: under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms, that drought caused greater water loss in cacao agroforests than in open-sun cacao because trees and cacao both transpire, and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_9, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8], and earlier work cited in a German alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of competition [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; the Ghana shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_1, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. Only those units and the cocoa and coffee review statements record a tree-perennial system; the Honduran, live-fence, FMNR, Ethiopian, Nigerian, understorey and shelterbelt units record none and are applied here by default [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_3, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_ieg20_4, ev_household_income_watts22_14, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. On the competing side, reviews cite that under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms, that drought caused greater water loss in cacao agroforests than in open-sun cacao because trees and cacao both transpire, and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_9, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]. mitigation_mechanism: The silvopasture study in this cell compared silvopasture with non-grazed managed forest in Washington State, USA: silvopasture management reduced grass biomass, litter and duff depth, and the authors conclude that managing overstory, understory and grazing together can reduce fuel loads and potential wildfire risk [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5]. Rotational grazing removes understory biomass and herbaceous surface fuel, and the reduced, more variable overstory density has the potential to reduce fire frequency compared with other land uses [ev_t3_herbaceous_fuel_batcheler24_4, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. Rate of fire spread and burn severity correlate with litter and duff depth in this forest type, which is why the litter reduction matters for fire [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6]. Separately, a Kenyan compiler for farmer managed natural regeneration rates that tree cover can increase the risk of major wild fires, and that fire breaks should be considered for larger sites [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk].
caveats: None of this evidence can set the class. Every comparison is against the unmanaged state, non-grazed managed forest, while this cell asks how silvopasture compares with the open pasture of an agro-pastoral system [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5, ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8]. Against treeless pasture the reading changes: introducing trees adds woody material, litter and duff that open pasture does not have, so having less fuel than a forest does not mean having less fuel than the pasture the practice replaces. Read against that comparator, the fire-spread correlation with litter and duff depth would point to added risk rather than a reduction [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6]. The study is also from a high-income US setting in the Interior Columbia Basin, outside the LIC/LMIC target; only select fuel types fell (1-, 10-, 100- and 1000-h fuels were similar between the management systems), and the fire-frequency statement is a potential effect, not a measurement [ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. What would fill the gap is a fire-risk comparison (fuel load, fire frequency or burn severity) of silvopasture against treeless pasture, ideally in an LIC/LMIC agro-pastoral system. The Kenyan WOCAT rating is carried but cannot set the class either: it is a practitioner judgement, not a measurement, and as the only evidence from a different source it sits below the evidence floor, which needs another independent source or a measured finding [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk]. It concerns natural regeneration rather than silvopasture, but its direction agrees with the comparator argument above: added tree cover adds fuel, and the compiler recommends fire breaks for larger sites [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk].

mitigation_mechanism: Measured cooling reaches crops: midday air temperature under Faidherbia albida canopies on Ethiopian wheat farms was up to 6°C lower than in the open field, poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot days, and lower heat load under Populus deltoides in India raised wheat grain yield by 6.8% [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6]. In the same Ethiopian study, a crop model found that the lower temperature under F. albida shade raised simulated wheat yield when nitrogen was applied, but without applied N simulated yield was extremely small and did not respond to temperature [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. Silvopastoral systems cut heat stress in cattle: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it, and eucalyptus–brachiaria systems in Brazil reduced the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% against monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. For cattle, shade from live fences reduces heat stress, giving a more comfortable environment and supporting reproduction, weight gain and milk production [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3]. In a shade-by-drought experiment on cocoa in Ghana, sub-canopy temperatures were lower in shade than in full-sun plots [ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1]. A meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found summer air temperature 4.01% lower and relative humidity 13.45% higher in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. Reviews and syntheses report the same cooling more generally: over-storey shade moderates severe temperature (2–4°C) effects on understorey crops, tree shading can lower ambient temperature by 4°C and soil temperature by 6–10°C, agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress, shade trees buffer rising temperatures to stabilise coffee yields, and shade trees produce microclimates that buffer temperature fluctuations [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3]. In Senegal's Ferlo, air temperature under Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C against 26 °C to 42 °C outside, and access to the cool zones under trees reduces livestock heat stress and so raises animal productivity [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22]. In cocoa and coffee, a pantropical synthesis found mean temperature lower and daily maximum and minimum temperatures buffered in cocoa agroforestry against monocultures, a review cites shade trees reducing canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, and measurements in Costa Rican coffee found shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
caveats: Windbreak hedges in Senegal generally cause a slight temperature rise in the protected plots, with effects that vary by crop and growth stage [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. Most units report cooling or animal comfort, entering as components of heat-stress impact, and nearly all are reviews citing earlier studies. The yield and milk-production units apply to hot conditions only, and the German alley-cropping unit is high-income temperate evidence [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. The Ghanaian cocoa shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so it captures above-ground shading only and its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_microclimate_buffering_mensah23_1]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The milk gains mix relief from heat with extra foliage and fruit, so they are not a pure heat-stress effect [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. The shelterbelt cooling is a pooled meta-analysis result from upper-middle-income China, expressed as a modest percentage change in air temperature rather than a measured heat-stress loss [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. The Ethiopian cooling was measured on farm, but its yield link is modelled, and the model's null without applied N is among the no-benefit results in this row [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. The IPCC chapter that says shade trees can ameliorate rising stand temperatures for arabica coffee adds in the same sentence that the opposite can also be true [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; they report temperature rather than heat-stress losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].

mitigation_mechanism: Silvopastoral and pasture trees cut cattle heat stress: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1]. Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. For cattle, shade from live fences reduces heat stress, giving a more comfortable environment and supporting reproduction, weight gain and milk production [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].
caveats: The Latin American silvopastoral units come from pastoral rangeland; the general reviews are applied here by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. Most units are reviews citing earlier studies, and the milk and weight-gain figures are associations with shade rather than measured heat-stress losses avoided [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The milk gains mix relief from heat with extra foliage and fruit, so they are not a pure heat-stress effect [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].

Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. Shade over cocoa and coffee lowers the temperature the crop experiences. A pantropical synthesis of cocoa studies found that the shade-tree canopy reduces solar radiation, so mean temperature stays lower and daily maximum and minimum temperatures are buffered compared with monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. A review cites shade trees reducing canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, mitigating heat stress, and the IPCC notes that shade trees can ameliorate the rising stand temperatures that will significantly affect arabica coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. mitigation_mechanism: Drought kills the trees of the system and cuts its output. Severe drought can raise tree seedling mortality by 35 to 40% because seedlings cannot match transpiration demands [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_3]. In Colombia, droughts provoked by El Niño between 2015 and 2016 caused significant losses of trees planted by the project, and the area under the most recently planted intensive silvopastoral systems fell by 45 percent in the severe 2019 drought in a survey of 285 farms [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_5, ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4]. In cabruca cocoa agroforests in southern Bahia, Brazil, cocoa tree mortality was 15% during the El Niño event against under 1% normally, 7% of the 317 woody shade trees died, and potential yield fell from 242 to 26 kg/ha, an 89% reduction, still 83% lower nine months after the drought ended [ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_1, ev_establishment_survival_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1]. In Ghana, leguminous shade trees competed with the crop for soil water during severe drought, enhancing crop mortality compared with full sun [ev_tree_canopy_cover_ipccar6ch5_3].
caveats: Seedling and young-system losses dominate: the Colombian source notes established systems were more drought-resilient than traditional pastures while young ones are vulnerable in their initial years [ev_drought_hazard_cmscr20_4], and one cited study found drought did not increase seedling mortality, though growth was impaired [ev_tree_canopy_cover_watts22_4]. The Bahia cocoa losses carry no unshaded comparator, so they show the damage to the asset, not whether shade made it worse or better [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_1]. The Ghana unit is the IPCC chapter's second-hand reading; the chapter writes coffee but the cited study is on cocoa [ev_tree_canopy_cover_ipccar6ch5_3].
